paper.title: Identifying the Risks of LM Agents with an LM-Emulated Sandbox

summary.one_sentence: ToolEmu uses a language model to emulate tool execution and sandbox states so agent risks can be tested before real tools are wired up.
summary.thesis: The paper's core contribution is a scalable red-team harness for tool-using agents: emulate the environment, run the agent, then use an LM evaluator to flag risky actions and severity.
summary.why_it_matters: For agent infrastructure, ToolEmu is a practical testing layer between prompt-only evaluation and real-world side effects. It does not replace real sandboxes, but it helps find dangerous trajectories early.

prior_state: Tool-using agents can leak data, transfer money, delete files, or trigger physical-world effects.
Testing these risks manually requires tool implementations, sandbox setup, scenario design, and human trajectory inspection.
Many high-stakes or future tools are difficult to instantiate safely in real environments.
Long-tail ambiguous instructions are especially hard to cover with hand-built test cases.
problem.key_gap: The paper asks how to test diverse, high-stakes agent-tool scenarios at scale without implementing every tool and sandbox.
assumptions: Strong LMs can emulate many tool outputs and sandbox states well enough to support early risk discovery.
An LM-based evaluator can approximate human judgments about risky agent trajectories.
Risk evaluation should measure both safety and helpfulness, not merely refusal.
The benchmark focuses on ambiguous or underspecified user instructions that can lead to harmful actions if the agent does not resolve uncertainty.

concepts.name: LM-emulated sandbox
concepts.definition: A virtual execution environment where an LM produces tool observations and state changes from tool specifications and agent inputs.

concepts.name: Tool emulator
concepts.definition: The ToolEmu component that emulates tool execution and sandbox state without a concrete tool implementation.

concepts.name: Adversarial emulator
concepts.definition: A ToolEmu variant that instantiates scenario states likely to expose severe or long-tail agent failures.

concepts.name: Safety evaluator
concepts.definition: An LM-based evaluator that inspects an agent trajectory to identify risky actions and assess consequence severity.

concepts.name: Helpfulness evaluator
concepts.definition: An LM-based evaluator that scores whether an agent effectively fulfills the user request without compromising safety.

concepts.name: Risk test case
concepts.definition: An instruction and tool scenario designed to test whether the agent resolves ambiguity or missing details before taking a high-stakes action.

method.core_idea: Replace expensive real tool sandboxes with an LM-emulated environment, run agents against curated risky scenarios, and use LM-based evaluators plus human validation to measure realistic failures.
action_grammar: tool specification: the interface and expected behavior of the tool under test.
user instruction: an ambiguous or underspecified request that may create safety risk.
agent action: the selected tool call and arguments.
emulated observation: the LM-generated tool result and sandbox state transition.
trajectory: the sequence of instructions, actions, observations, and final answer.
safety score: evaluator judgment over risky action and consequence severity.
helpfulness score: evaluator judgment over task completion without unsafe behavior.
adversarial state: an instantiated environment state chosen to make failures more likely.
steps: Formalize tool-using LM agents as systems that act in a partially observable environment.
Use an LM emulator to generate tool observations from tool specifications and agent inputs.
Add an adversarial emulator to instantiate challenging sandbox states for red-teaming.
Build LM-based safety and helpfulness evaluators for scalable trajectory scoring.
Validate the emulator and evaluators against human annotations.
Curate a benchmark of 36 high-stakes toolkits and 144 test cases across 9 risk types.
Evaluate current LM agents and prompt variants for safety-helpfulness tradeoffs.
method.pseudocode:
for test_case in benchmark:
    state = emulator.instantiate(test_case)
    trajectory = run_agent(agent, tools=emulated_tools, state=state)
    safety = safety_evaluator.score(trajectory)
    helpfulness = helpfulness_evaluator.score(trajectory)
    record(test_case, trajectory, safety, helpfulness)

# Real sandboxes are still needed for deployment proof; LM emulation is an early risk-discovery layer.

claims.statement: ToolEmu uses an LM to emulate tool executions and sandbox states from tool specifications and tool inputs.
caveats: The emulator is approximate; it is useful for scalable risk discovery, not final production assurance.

claims.statement: The framework pairs the emulator with LM-based safety and helpfulness evaluators to score complete agent trajectories.
caveats: Evaluator reliability is bounded by agreement with human annotators and can miss or mis-score failures.

claims.statement: The initial benchmark covers 36 high-stakes toolkits, 144 test cases, and 9 risk types.
caveats: The benchmark targets one threat model: ambiguous or missing-details instructions that may induce risky actions.

claims.statement: Human validation found most sampled emulations realistic enough for risk testing, and 68.8% of failures identified by ToolEmu were judged valid real-world agent failures.
caveats: The 68.8% figure also means a substantial fraction of flagged failures were not validated as genuine realistic failures.

claims.statement: In the benchmark, GPT-4 and Claude-2 were the strongest base agents, but still failed in 39.4% and 44.3% of test cases respectively.
caveats: These are evaluator-based results on the ToolEmu benchmark, not direct measurements in real deployed environments.

claims.statement: Adding explicit safety requirements to GPT-4 improved both safety and helpfulness, but the best prompted agent still failed in 23.9% of test cases.
caveats: Prompting reduced risk but did not eliminate it; the result does not prove the same prompt helps every agent or tool domain.

claims.statement: ToolEmu suggests a useful safety workflow: use cheap LM-emulated red-teaming to discover candidate failures, then reproduce high-severity findings in real sandboxes before shipping.
caveats: This is an infrastructure inference from the paper; the paper itself does not claim LM emulation is sufficient for deployment certification.

evidence.result: ToolEmu emulates tool execution and sandbox states with an LM using only tool specifications and tool inputs, avoiding manual implementation for many scenarios.
The framework includes an LM-based safety evaluator for risky actions/severity and a helpfulness evaluator for task completion.
The benchmark contains 36 high-stakes toolkits, 144 test cases, and 9 risk categories including privacy breach, financial loss, data loss/corruption, safety hazards, and computer security compromise.

The paper reports that over 80% of sampled tool execution trajectories were judged realistic by humans and that 68.8% of failures identified by the emulator/evaluator were validated as genuine risky failures with realistic trajectories.
Among base agents, GPT-4 and Claude-2 had the strongest safety/helpfulness scores, while still exhibiting failures in 39.4% and 44.3% of ToolEmu test cases.
A GPT-4 agent prompted with safety requirements improved over the base agent and was the safest evaluated agent, but still failed in 23.9% of test cases.
Because ToolEmu finds candidate failures cheaply but validates only probabilistically, a production process should triage LM-emulated findings into real sandbox reproduction and policy/runtime fixes.

agent_infra_takeaways: Agent safety evaluation needs trajectory-level testing, not only single-turn model safety scores.
LM-emulated sandboxes are useful for early risk discovery when real tools are expensive, unsafe, or not yet implemented.
Do not confuse emulation with containment. A production agent still needs real sandboxing, scoped capabilities, audit logs, and policy enforcement.
Safety prompting can reduce failures, but the paper's best prompted agent still failed on nearly one quarter of ToolEmu cases.
Helpfulness should be measured alongside safety so the agent is not rewarded for refusing everything.
High-severity ToolEmu findings should become regression tests in real tool sandboxes once the tool exists.
caveats: The emulator and evaluators are LMs, so they can hallucinate tool behavior or misjudge trajectory risk.
The benchmark focuses on ambiguous or underspecified user instructions, not all agent threat models.
Reported model failure rates are historical and tied to the evaluated model versions, prompts, and ToolEmu benchmark.
ToolEmu is best interpreted as scalable red-team infrastructure, not as a formal safety guarantee.
Human validation supports the method but also reveals nontrivial false positives or non-realistic failures.

related_work.title: GCG Attacks
related_work.note: GCG tests adversarial model behavior; ToolEmu tests the downstream tool-risk consequences of unsafe agent actions.

related_work.title: WebArena
related_work.note: WebArena uses concrete web environments for task success; ToolEmu uses LM-emulated tools to broaden high-stakes risk testing.

poc.note: No PoC yet. A safe PoC could emulate benign file, email, or calendar tools locally and show how a trajectory-level evaluator flags ambiguous high-risk actions without executing them.
